## The Same Thirteen Salaries, in R {.sim-slide #mm-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 2 · Descriptive statistics
:::

::: {.lede-min}
Every summary you just watched is one line of R.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
pay <- c(38, 42, 45, 47, 49, 50,
         50, 50, 52, 54, 56, 59, 
         62)

# Descriptive statistics
sort(table(pay), decreasing = TRUE)[1] # mode
range(pay)   # 38 and 62
median(pay)  # the 7th value once sorted
mean(pay)    # 654 / 13
var(pay)     # divisor is n - 1, not n
sd(pay)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Change the last salary to `96` and run it again. The mode and the median count positions, so they do not move; the mean and the standard deviation measure distances, so they do.
:::


## A Bound that Holds for *Any* Shape {.sim-slide #cheb-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 2 · Chebyshev
:::

::: {.lede-min}
Chebyshev promises at least $1 - 1/k^2$ of any distribution lies within $k$ standard deviations. No normality, no symmetry, no assumptions at all.
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
k <- 2 # <-- how many SDs
n <- 20000

# a wildly skewed population, far from normal
x  <- rexp(n, rate = 1) ^ 2
mu <- mean(x); s <- sd(x)

actual <- mean(abs(x - mu) <= k * s)
bound  <- 1 - (1 / k) ^ 2
round(c(actual = actual, chebyshev = bound), 3)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The bound holds, but loosely — that is the price of assuming nothing. Swap `rexp(n, 1)^2` for `rnorm(n)` and the gap widens further: for a normal, $k = 2$ captures 95%, not the 75% Chebyshev guarantees.
:::
